choices.text: Plants only respire at night, because photosynthesis replaces respiration by day
Plants respire only in bright light, when energy is available
Plants respire around the clock, day and night
Plants never respire, because they make their own food

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Plants only respire at night. During the day photosynthesis dominates, so respiration looks switched off. Plants respire around the clock: at night there is simply no photosynthesis to hide it, as scene s2 shows.
questions.prompt: A student says a green plant only respires when it is dark. What is correct?

choices.text: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy

questions.explanation: Scene s2 gives the aerobic respiration equation: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy, yielding about 32 ATP per glucose.
questions.prompt: Which is the correct word equation for aerobic respiration?

questions.answer: The folds give a huge surface area for respiratory enzymes, so more aerobic respiration and more ATP production can happen.
questions.explanation: Scene s1 shows cristae folding the inner membrane: folding means huge surface area, so more ATP is made.
questions.prompt: Explain why the folded cristae of a mitochondrion help it make more ATP.

questions.answer: Yeast: ethanol + carbon dioxide. Muscle: lactic acid. Both yield far less ATP than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partly broken down.
questions.explanation: Scene s4 forks one glucose two ways: yeast to ethanol + CO2, muscle to lactic acid, with far less ATP than aerobic either way.
questions.prompt: Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast and in muscle: name the products of each and state the ATP yield compared with aerobic respiration.

choices.text: The Calvin cycle, from carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Scene s5 shows photolysis splitting water in the thylakoids and releasing oxygen, while the Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide into glucose.
questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, the oxygen released comes from which process and source?
